Effects of biological pretreatments of microalgae on hydrolysis, biomethane 
potential and microbial community 
Mekdimu Mezemir Damtie a,1, Jingyeong Shin a,1, Hyun Min Jang b, Hyun Uk Cho c, 
Jinhua Wang d, Young Mo Kim a,* 
a Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Hanyang University, Seongdong-gu, Seoul 04763, Republic of Korea 
b Department of Environment & Energy and Soil Environment Research Center, Jeonbuk National University, Jeonju, Jeollabukdo 57896, Republic of Korea 
c Department of Marine Environmental Engineering, Gyeongsang National University, Tongyeong, Gyeongnam 53064, Republic of Korea 
d College of Resources and Environment, Shandong Agricultural University, Tai’an 271018, China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
• Hydrolysis and BMP performance of various biological pretreatments were studied. 
• Different pretreatment conditions have resulted in different microbial diversity. 
• PCA analysis identified no correlation between hydrolysis and BMP. 
• BMP showed good correlation with sN, sP, sCOD, and propionic acid formation. 
• Total VFAs were correlated to VS removal and levels of acetic and butyric acid.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Temperature-phased anaerobic digestion 
Microalgae 
Biomethane potential 
Volatile fatty acids 
Microbial community 
A B S T R A C T   
Parameters of temperature-phased anaerobic digestion (TPAD) were varied to study their effects on hydrolysis, 
biomethane potential (BMP), and microbial diversity of microalgae biodegradation. Anaerobic pretreatments at 
85 ◦C demonstrated the release of soluble carbohydrate and protein molecules under low microbial metabolic 
activity. However, at 55 ◦C, anaerobic pretreatments showed superior performance in methane yield, nutrient 
release, and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) production due to dominant Clostridium. Furthermore, the highest 
destruction of volatile solids (VS) was observed during aerobic pretreatments at 55 ◦C under the influence of 
various quantities of these genera – Luteimonas, Symbiobacterium, Soehngenia, Thermobacillus, and Ureibacillus. 
Statistical analysis revealed that hydrolysis and BMP were not correlated. However, soluble nitrogen and 
phosphorous showed strong correlation with methane (r = 0.623 and 0.948, respectively) under thermo- 
anaerobic pretreatment, while VS removal and concentrations of acetic and butyric acids and lipids were posi­
tively correlated with each other under thermo-aerobic pretreatment.   
1. Introduction 
As a potential alternative energy source to fossil fuels, third-gen­
eration biofuels derived from microalgae have shown promise for bio- 
energy production due to their high quantum yield, high biomass per 
unit area, and low competition for arable land (Marsolek et al., 2014). 
Growing algae using wastewater effluent offers multiple benefits such as 
the recovery of nutrients, removal of heavy metals, and production of 
biogas as a renewable energy source. It also has the potential of coupling 
CO2 mitigation to wastewater recycling (Barrag´an-Trinidad et al., 
2017). 
However, digestion of algae requires pretreatment to breakdown 
resistant cell walls to render them susceptible to microbial attack 
(Gonzalez-Fernandez et al., 2015). Various technologies have been 
suggested as pretreatment including physical, thermal, chemical, me­
chanical, and biological processes (Passos et al., 2014). Biological 
degradation of microalgae using anaerobic digestion offers the most 
cost-effective, environmental-friendly option, is feasible for large-scale

application, and is energy-efficient, requiring few chemicals, while 
producing non-inhibitory byproducts (Sindhu et al., 2016). It requires 
microorganisms such as fungi, protozoa, and bacteria, and costly in­
dustrial enzymatic cocktails (Barrag´an-Trinidad et al., 2017). 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is generally regarded as a potential means 
to recovery energy via biogas production. Among the various types of 
AD setups, the current study utilized temperature-phased anaerobic 
digestion (TPAD) due to its excellent reactor stability, methanogen ac­
tivity, and the abundance and diversity of the microbial community (Ge 
et al., 2011; Jang et al., 2014). The biggest advantage of TPAD is its 
potential to combine both enhanced hydrolysis and stability while uti­
lizing moderate energy input and completely removing pathogens 
(Pervin et al., 2013). Moreover, TPAD provides both high destruction of 
solids along with an increased rate of gas production at a relatively low 
capital cost (Ge et al., 2011). This increased removal of volatile solids 
(VS) thereby reduces the costs associated with subsequent sludge dew­
atering and sludge disposal (Lv et al., 2010). 
However, applications of these biological methods to microalgae 
pretreatment have been limited, to date, due to insufficient knowledge 
and uncertainties about the process performance. Among these, the 
literature reveals insufficient studies to demonstrate hydrolysis, VFAs 
formation, and BMP capabilities of different TPAD systems during 
microalgae digestion. Moreover, understanding the correlations be­
tween these factors helps to optimize as well as indirectly estimate BMP 
and VFAs which would otherwise require us to employ tedious, expen­
sive, and time-consuming laboratory procedures. Moreover, much re­
mains unknown about the relationship between the dynamics of 
microbial diversity and biological pretreatments while varying hy­
draulic retention time (HRT), temperature, and redox conditions (Lv 
et al., 2010). The scientific literature contains several related studies 
that applied statistical approaches. Perendeci et al. (2019) considered 
various substrate compositions including glucose, Kjeldahl nitrogen, 
and chlorophyll in the mesophilic co-digestion of microalgae to create 
statistical relationships with BMP. Lesteur et al. (2010) correlated BMP 
of mesophilic biodegradation with elemental and biochemical compo­
sition. Magdalena et al. (2019) employed organic loading rate and 
ammonia concentration to observe the production rate of VFAs from 
microalgae digestion under mesophilic conditions. Very few studies 
have comparied performance and application of different thermophilic 
pretreatment phases of TPAD for microalgae digestion. Zamorano-L´opez 
et al. (2019) studied microbial dynamics and its statistical correlation 
with organic loading rate and free ammonia in a TPAD system. Some 
studies addressed the effect of pretreatment temperature in TPAD (Ge 
et al., 2011) while others compared the BMP potential of TPAD and 
mesophilic conditions (Zhang et al., 2019). However, to the best of our 
knowledge, there has been no comprehensive study comparing the 
pretreatment performance of different TPAD-based biological pre­
treatments of microalgae, and no study has clearly identified indicators 
to estimate the extent of hydrolysis, tendency of VFAs formation, and 
BMP through considering their interactions with the underlying micro­
bial community. 
The main objective of this study was, therefore, to investigate the 
performance of different TPAD systems under variable temperatures, 
HRTs, and redox conditions and statistically compare their response for 
identification of parameters sufficiently correlated to forecast and 
optimize hydrolysis propensity, VFAs production and BMP estimation of 
microalgae biodegradation. This study uniquely provides extensive in­
formation on the microbiomes of different thermophilic pretreatment 
systems, substrate physicochemical properties, and biodegradation re­
sponses all in one factorial plane allowing a comprehensive overview of 
their correlation, interaction, and comparison with different biological 
pretreatments of microalgae including the thermo-aerobic process 
which has not previously been dealt with in detail. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Microalgal biomass and the inoculum 
The Chlorella vulgaris microalgae biomass utilized as a substrate in 
this study was cultivated in freshwater and purchased from Daesang 
Corporation, Korea. The biomass was grown in complete darkness at a 
temperature of 30 ◦C and aerated using air spargers at a flow rate of 1 L/ 
min while being continuously agitated at a speed of 90 rpm. To facilitate 
production, microalgae growth was assisted using 8–10% liquid sugar. 
The pH of the algae growth media was maintained between 7.5 and 8.0. 
During pretreatment, a semi-continuous mode setup was established and 
tap water had been utilized to dilute the microalgae samples due to their 
high concentration of total solids (TS). The inoculum for microalgae 
pretreatment was acquired from a full-scale mesophilic anaerobic 
digester at the Gwangju municipal wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) 
(Gwangju, Korea). For pretreatment under aerobic conditions, the 
inoculum was obtained from activated sludge in the secondary treat­
ment of the same plant. Detailed characteristics of the raw microalgae 
and inocula are shown in Table 1. 
2.2. Microalgae pretreatment (first phase of TPAD) 
Raw microalgae were diluted twice and the pH was set to 7.0 before 
starting the experiment. Then, the microalgae as a substrate were semi- 
continuously fed into the reactor in a thermophilic, continuously stirred 
5 L tank reactor having a working volume of 2.8 L and was operated for 
908 h. This duration refers to the time consumed for the entire operation 
beginning with the start-up and adaptation phase (0 to 300 h), then 
pretreatment at an HRT of 3 days (300 to 624 h), pretreatment at an HRT 
of 2 days (624 to 792 h), and pretreatment at an HRT of 1 day (792 to 
908 h). See the time boundaries in Fig. 1. The continuous agitation 
stirring speed was 150 rpm. To maintain aerobic conditions, an initial 
flow rate of 5 L/min was achieved by the air spargers to aerate the 
reactor, then was continuously increased until bubbles were formed at a 
flow rate of 10 L/min. For establishing anaerobic conditions, the reactor 
was purged once with nitrogen at the beginning of the experiment. To 
change the temperature in the reactor, heating tape was used. The 
experiment was started in such a way that, originally, the anaerobic 
conditions were set at 85 ◦C, 70 ◦C, and 55 ◦C. The assay from 70 ◦C was 
ultimately omitted from the checklist since there was no significant 
difference between its results and those from 85 ◦C and 70 ◦C. Anaerobic 
conditions at 85 ◦C and 55 ◦C were finally selected and run at 3 different 
hydraulic retention times (HRTs) (3 days, 2 days, and 1 day). Then, the 
operation was carried out under aerobic conditions at 55 ◦C using the 
same HRTs (3 days, 2 days, and 1 day). A syringe was used to take 
digested microalgae samples 2 to 3 times a day with sample volumes of 
450 to 900 mL depending on the HRTs. All data were collected either in 
duplicate or triplicate and the average and standard error values were 
recorded. After completion of the microalgae pretreatment, BMP was

2.3. Biochemical methane potential assay (Second phase of TPAD) 
The AD of untreated microalgae was set as a reference to measure 
methane yield. Both raw and pretreated microalgae were tested under 
12 different pretreatment conditions in a semi-continuous mode. During 
the biochemical methane potential experiment, the biologically pre­
treated microalgae were digested in a 250 mL serum bottle with a 
working volume of 150 mL. The ratio of VS-based inoculum to pre­
treated microalgae in the reactor was 2:1 and the initial pH was 7. 
Mesophilic conditions were established by adjusting the temperature to 
35 ◦C and flushing the headspace with nitrogen gas. The test bottles 
were completely plugged with stoppers and placed on a shaking incu­
bator running at 150 rpm. The BMP tests continued until the methane 
production completely stopped which required approximately 35 days. 
The digested microalgae samples were collected using a syringe twice a 
day and methane production was immediately measured. Data for each 
condition were collected both in a duplicate experiment and duplicate 
measurement. In addition to the methane yield, VS, soluble chemical 
oxygen demand (sCOD) and VFAs were also carefully recorded for each 
condition. Moreover, to clearly understand the methane yield and pro­
duction rate, experimentally collected values of methane yields were 
modeled using a modified Gompertz equation as this model has an 
excellent capability to precisely forecast the lag phase which results 
mainly from the digestion of highly recalcitrant lignocellulosic biomass 
(Bohutskyi et al., 2018). The modified Gompertz equation is shown in

2.4. Analytical procedures and devices 
Standard methods (APHA/AWWA/WEF, 2018) were employed to 
measure the TS, VS, total nitrogen (T-N), and total phosphorus (T-P). For 
analysis of soluble total phosphorus (sP), soluble total nitrogen (sN), 
ammonium (NH4
+-N), and sCOD, samples were first filtered by using a 
0.45 μm pore size filter and then analyzed by standard methods. tCOD 
measurement was conducted using the tCOD-chromium standard 
method following procedures described in ASTM D1252-95 (1995). 
Carbohydrates were measured using the phenol–sulfuric acid 
method. This involves preparing 1 mL of sample in a test tube and 
adding 1 mL of double-distilled (dd) water, then mixing it with 0.05 mL 
80% phenol. Then to each tube, 5.0 mL H2SO4 was rapidly added and 
mixed by a vortex test tube mixer. The samples were left to stand for 10 
min and then placed in a 25 ◦C bath for another 10 min followed by an 
additional vortex. The final samples were then transferred to cuvettes 
and taken for reading the absorbance (at 470 nm spectra) against 
standard curve tubes which had been prepared using standard 100 mg 
glucose/L solution and dd water. Detailed procedures were taken from 
Nielsen (2010). 
To determine protein concentrations, the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) 
method was employed using a Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit from 
Thermo Scientific for application in the test tube procedure (Thermo 
Fisher Scientific Firm, 2009). The sample to working reagent (WR) ratio 
was 1:20. In this procedure, 0.1 mL of unknown sample replicates and 
standard samples were first mixed well with 2.0 mL of the WR in each 
tube. The tubes were then covered and incubated at 37 ◦C for 30 min and 
cooled. Then the absorbance of all the samples was measured within 10 
min with the spectrophotometer set to 562 nm. The average 562 nm 
absorbance measurement of the blank standard replicates was sub­
tracted from the 562 nm absorbance measurement of all other individual 
standard and unknown sample replicates. Then the protein concentra­
tions of each unknown sample were read from the standard curve. Lipid 
concentrations were analyzed using gravimetry after extraction of lipids 
by solvents (chloroform: methanol, 1:2 v/v). For analyzing VFAs, a gas 
chromatograph (GC) (model YL6500 GC, Young Lin Instrument Co., 
Anyang-si, Korea) was used. To measure methane, total biogas volume 
was first determined and then multiplied by the percentage composition 
of methane (%) in the biogas which had been estimated from the gas 
chromatograph device stated above. To measure biogas volume, a water 
displacement method was employed after collecting the biogas samples 
in a two-liter, plastic Tedlar bag. In this biogas measuring technique, the 
volume of displaced water was assumed to be equal to the biogas vol­
ume. But corrections of biogas volumes to standard conditions have 
been applied to eliminate uncertainties induced due to information 
missing from different environmental factors such as temperature, 
pressure, water vapor and headspace composition. The method 
described in Str¨omberg et al. (2014) was used to calculate the adjust­
ment factor even though the errors observed were not significant. Ori­
ginPro2016 compatible with Windows® 10 was employed to fit the data 
and estimate correlation coefficients (r2) as well as to make graphs and

2.5. Microbial community analysis 
Microbial communities were identified using the Illumina iSeq 100 
sequencing system instructions (Illumina, CA, USA). The selected 16S 
rRNA gene region-specific sequences used as amplicon primers and the 
bacterial primers were 518F (5′-CCAGCAGCCGCGGTAATACG-3′) and 
805R (5′- GACTACCAGGGTATCTAATCC-3′) targeting the V3-V4 region 
for bacteria (Yu et al., 2005). The DNA were PCR-amplified with the 
annealing temperature set to 58 ◦C and purified for construction of the 
library. The library was then paired-end (150 bp × 2) sequenced using 
the iSeq 100 platform. The paired reads were then merged and further 
processed by using short and low-quality sequences to reduce potential 
error. Operational taxonomic units were defined at a 97% sequence 
identity cutoff. According to the read, initially, a total of 65,368 to 
94,706 sequence reads at the kingdom level were generated by 
sequencing 16S rRNA gene from 12 digester sludge samples. A total of 
24 phyla, 47 classes, 100 orders, 221 families, and 588 genera were 
monitored from the total sequence reads. PCoA was also performed to 
visualize the similarity and dissimilarity of microbial community 
structures within and among the digesters based on the relative abun­
dances of OTUs obtained from 12 different digester pretreatment sam­
ples. Moreover, a Circos graph showing the relationship between the 
pretreatment methods and their respective microbial abundance was 
constructed using Circos Table Viewer v0.63-9 © 2008-2020 (Krzy­
winski et al., 2009). 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of pretreatment on microalgae hydrolysis 
3.1.1. Release of organic macromolecules 
Three pretreatment conditions (anaerobic pretreatment at 85 ◦C, 
anaerobic at 55 ◦C, and aerobic at 55 ◦C) at three different HRTs (3, 2, 
and 1 day) were selected to study the effects of biological pretreatment 
of microalgae on the release of macromolecules. As compared to the 
original concentrations of carbohydrate measured in the non-treated 
raw microalgae control sample (the diluted version of table 1), an 
average of 16-fold carbohydrate release was obtained from anaerobic 
pretreatment at 85 ◦C at an HRT of 3 days (Fig. 1a). For the 55 ◦C 
anaerobic and aerobic pretreatments, the average carbohydrates release 
was 13-fold and 7-fold, respectively. Similarly, the average protein 
release (Fig. 1b) at an HRT of 3 days at 85 ◦C anaerobic, 55 ◦C anaerobic, 
and 55 ◦C aerobic pretreatments increased by 10-fold, 6-fold, and 3-fold, 
respectively, compared to their initial control values. These trials 
showed that 85 ◦C was relatively the better temperature and anaerobic 
was the better redox condition, and longer HRTs such as 3 days were the 
optimum retention times for the highest releases of carbohydrates and 
proteins. Such variations in performance might be attributable to dif­
ferences in their microbial activity because at 85 ◦C there was release 
only of soluble macromolecules with no further biodegradation; on the 
other hand, at 55 ◦C the relative amount of carbohydrate concentration 
was quite low due to an active thermophilic biological process which 
further consumed and/or decomposed the carbohydrates into interme­
diate products such as VFAs (Sol´e-Bund´o et al., 2017). Under aerobic 
conditions, there might also be high microbial activity consuming sol­
uble organics and producing CO2, which may explain why the lowest 
concentration of such macromolecules occurred in aerobic conditions. 
E-supplementary data regarding VS removal can be found in the online 
version of this paper. On the other hand, the highest release of lipids was 
obtained at 55 ◦C during aerobic pretreatment at an HRT of 3 days 
(Fig. 1c), showing an average of 2-fold increment as compared to its 
initial lipids concentration in the control emphasizing that lipids release 
was linked mainly to the degree of microbial activity which can release 
both intracellular and extracellular materials rather than to the thermal 
effect which mainly avails lipids from the extracellular media (Sol´e- 
Bund´o et al., 2017). 
3.1.2. Volatile fatty acids 
The VFAs generated during AD in this study included acetic acid 
(C2), propionic acid (C3), butyric acid (C4), and valeric acid (C5). As per 
results from the anaerobic pretreatment at 85 ◦C (Fig. 2a), a substantial 
amount of long-chain VFAs such as valeric and isovaleric acids were 
produced, whereas at 55 ◦C (both anaerobic and aerobic), the compo­
sition was dominated by short-chain VFAs such as acetic, butyric, and 
propionic acids (see Fig. 2b). Furthermore, concentrations of the VFAs 
more than doubled in 55 ◦C anaerobic pretreatments at an HRT of 1 day 
(5.3 g/L) as compared to 85 ◦C anaerobic at an HRT of 1 day (2.3 g/L). 
These differences might be ascribed to microbial hydrolysis activity in 
that at hyper-thermophilic temperatures, solubilization could be the 
result of physicochemical factors, while at thermophilic temperatures, 
there are biological factors from the action of microbial enzymes. 
Temperature is generally a vital parameter in acidogenesis due to its 
direct contribution both to microbial growth and system metabolism 
(Wainaina et al., 2019). 
In aerobic pretreatment, the quantity and structure of the VFAs 
spectrum significantly changed. In anaerobic pretreatment, released 
organic substances from the disruption of cell walls continue to accu­
mulate as VFAs, and any further retention of the substrate yields even 
relatively more short-chain VFAs. On the other hand, in the aerobic 
process, once soluble organics and short-chain VFAs are formed, the 
microbes tend to consume and form CO2 and greatly reduce the con­
centration of short-chain VFAs. This is one reason why the magnitude of 
total VFAs in the aerobic digester was also significantly less than under 
anaerobic conditions (Fig. 2c,d). The second reason for considerably 
higher VFAs formation in anaerobic than in aerobic pretreatment might 
be linked to microbial diversity and abundance. It is generally recog­
nized that the phyla Firmicutes and Thermotogae are highly correlated 
with VFAs formation (Lin et al., 2017). Microbes detected in aerobic 
pretreatments are mainly heterotrophic bacteria with tendencies that 
stimulate the digestion of slowly biodegradable compounds through 
exoenzymes, resulting in highly destructed VS and VFAs being con­
verted to CO2 (See detailed microbial discussions in Section 3.3). The 
most dominant VFAs in anaerobic pretreatment were acetic and propi­
onic acids which formed a high concentration of short-chain VFAs 
(Fig. 2d). Under aerobic conditions, butyric acid was the predominant 
VFA (Fig. 2c) because the system initially accumulates a substantial 
amount of acetic acid for ATP production but this excess accumulation 
might induce microbes to activate reverse fermentation which ulti­
mately converts acetic acid to butyric and propionic acids (Fig. 1c) (Jin 
et al., 2016). In addition, high concentrations of butyric acid and other 
long-chain VFAs under aerobic conditions might be attributable to the 
high concentrations of lipids released during the aerobic pretreatment 
from disruption of algae that changes lipid molecules to long-chain fatty 
acids by microbial action. 
The effect of HRTs on VFAs formation was also studied. At 85 ◦C, 
there was relatively more concentration of short-chain VFAs at an HRT 
of 3 days (Fig. 2a) because longer HRTs in hyper-thermophilic working 
temperatures might lead to an increase in the rate of hydrolysis, making 
hydroxylates theoretically available for fermentative microbial meta­
bolism (Wainaina et al., 2019). Moreover, maintaining the substrate at 
high temperatures for an extended period favors further degradation of 
the long-chain VFAs. 
3.1.3. Biomethanization 
As can be seen from the experimental results in Fig. 3, each pre­
treatment technique offers its unique features with regards to bio­
methanization. E-supplementary data of the modeling work can be 
found in the online version of the paper. Anaerobic pretreatment at 85 
◦C showed the highest methane yield (Go = 239.93 mL/g-VSadded); 
anaerobic pretreatment at 55 ◦C had the highest rate of methane yield

5
(Rmax = 30.7 mL/g-VSadded/day); and aerobic pretreatment at 55 ◦C 
resulted in the smallest lag-time (λ = 0.06 days). Because of the very 
high rate of methane production at anaerobic pretreatment at 55 ◦C, one 
would speculate a priori that the highest methane yield would have been 
observed at 55 ◦C. However, the decline at an HRT of 3 days might be 
due to the long HRT employed in which methane production had 
already been partially started and squandered during the pretreatment 
stage. On the other hand, the methane yield reduction at an HRT of 3 
days after aerobic pretreatment might reflect the sudden change in 
redox or microbial composition (Section 3.3) or the loss of the solubi­
lized organics by biodegradation. Another reason for reduction of 
methane in aerobic pretreatment may be due to the inhibition of 
methane production caused by the formation of intermediate products 
such as long-chain VFAs from lipid molecules (Ward et al., 2014). The 
results showed that the methane yields generally appeared to correlate 
strongly with the HRT and each pretreatment had its own optimal HRT. 
Those with very rapid biological activities required shorter HRTs. In our 
study, at an HRT of 2 days, a maximum methane yield enhancement up 
to 45%, 54%, and 36% was observed from aerobic pretreatment at 55 
◦C, anaerobic pretreatment at 55 ◦C, and anaerobic at 85 ◦C, respec­
tively, as compared to the samples without any pretreatment. Similar 
methane enhancement (nearly 55%) has also been observed from pri­
mary sludge digestion (Sol´e-Bund´o et al., 2019). 
3.2. Effect of pretreatment on the interrelationship between 
environmental factors 
Two PCAs accounting for approximately 68% of total variance were 
considered (Fig. 4). The first principal component (PC1) expressed 
43.1% of the overall variance. Parameters linked to PC1 were total 
VFAs, acetic acid, lipids, removed VS, and butyric acid which are posi­
tively correlated with each other but negatively affected by proteins, 
carbohydrates, valeric acid, isovaleric acid, and isobutyric acid, all of 
which overlapped and correlated well with each other. PC2 represented 
24.9% of variability and showed a strong correlation with factors such as 
propionic acid, sN, sP, methane yield, ammonia, and sCOD which also 
correlated with each other. Loading all the pretreatment methods on the 
factorial plane described by PC1 versus PC2 formed different clusters. 
The distance between each point describes the strength/weakness of 
correlation and also emphasizes the importance of the redox condition, 
HRT, and temperature. Based on the dominant background process, the 
clusters were named as a hyper-thermo-anaerobic cluster (green dots of 
AnH1, AnH2, and AnH3), thermo-anaerobic cluster (black dots of AnT2 
and AnT3), and thermo-aerobic cluster (red dots of AT1, AT2, AT3, and 
AnT1). Results obtained from an HRT of day 1, especially in the thermo- 
clusters, were erroneous and were excluded from the discussion because 
of their uncertainty. Normally, too short a HRT may cause incomplete 
substrate degradation or microbial death by starvation and may not 
represent reliable data (Magdalena et al., 2019). 
The hyper-thermo-anaerobic cluster can best be explained by car­

other. This confirms the findings of Passos et al. (2013) that pretreat­
ment at high temperature (85 ◦C) succeeded in solubilizing compounds 
that remained intact when a lower temperature (55 ◦C) was applied. 
Normally, microalgae are not likely to disintegrate at 70–90 ◦C but 
temperatures in this range enhance methane yield by partial weakening 
and breaking down cell walls and releasing macromolecules (Passos 
et al., 2014). The slow soluble organic consumption induced by weak 
microbial activity also favors the accumulation of these macromole­
cules. An interesting observation is that when long-chain VFAs (iso- 
valeric, iso-butyric, and valeric acids) were produced, total VFAs were 
reduced. This is because the formation of long-chain VFAs in the reactor 
was a clear indication of the presence of some internal/external inhib­
iting factors that slow down the entire biodegradation process which, in 
turn, affected total VFAs as well. In addition, the long-chain VFAs 
themselves can also inhibit acetogenesis, thereby decreasing acetic acid 
and leading to a decrease in total VFAs. This interpretation could be 
supported by the current PCA result (Fig. 4) in which acetic acid had a 
strong correlation with total VFAs. 
The thermo-aerobic cluster was best explained by butyric acid, 
lipids, acetic acid, total VFAs, and VS removal implying that aerobic 
conditions are a relatively good choice if the lipids and total VFAs were 
estimated. The highest accumulation of lipids in the aerobic pretreat­
ment might be attributable to a lack of lipid digesting microbes (e,g 
Bacteroidetes). The high VS destruction was due to improved solubility of 
the organic matter by aerobic conditions that rapidly avail biodegrad­
able organic matter to the oxidizing biomass (Montalvo et al., 2016) 
such as Symbiobacterium, Soehngenia, and Ureibacillus (Section 3.3). Due 
to high reduction of VS under thermo-aerobic conditions, such a pre­
treatment protocol is generally not an appropriate technology for 
methane production as the microbes convert the soluble organics to CO2 
gas; otherwise, relatively short HRTs need to be employed for the pre­
treatment. This is also the reason for the lack of correlation observed 
between removal of VS and methane yield in the thermo-anaerobic 
cluster. On the other hand, aerobic pretreatment is advantageous, 
being a powerful rapid process with the pH and temperature 
environment conducive to biomethanization (Jang et al., 2014). 
Even though the highest concentration of total VFAs was recorded 
under thermo-anaerobic conditions, no correlation was observed be­
tween the thermo-anaerobic cluster and total VFAs in the PCA analysis. 
This reflects the total VFAs being highly dominated by the butyric acid 
concentration which had been abundantly formed in the thermo-aerobic 
pretreatment. The strong correlation between the thermo-aerobic clus­
ter and butyric acid may be due to higher hydrogen partial pressure 
formation in the system. Usually, butyric acid accumulates in the system 
when hydrogen-utilizing microbes are exposed to partial pressures 
above 10−4 atm (Magdalena et al., 2019). In our experiment, excess 
butyric acid thus formed a strong correlation between the thermo- 
aerobic pretreatment and total VFAs because over 71% of the total 
VFAs originated from the butyric acid. The remainder of the total VFAs 
was metabolized mainly to acetic acid (21%) which also correlates well 
with the thermos-aerobic pretreatment. In aerated reactors like AT2 and 
AT3, syntrophic propionate oxidation (SPO) is highly favored and 
microaeration enhanced the oxidation of propionate to acetate and 
stimulated the formation of high acetic acid concentration (Lim and 
Wang, 2013) even though part of it was later converted to butyric acid 
during the reverse fermentation process. This butyric-acetic interaction 
and accumulation was responsible for the strong correlation between 
acetic and butyric acids in the thermo-aerobic cluster. On the other 
hand, propionic acid formation was correlated more with the thermo- 
anaerobic cluster than the thermo-aerobic cluster. This is mainly 
because the free ammonia nitrogen accumulation in AnT2 and AnT3 was 
less than the inhibition level; thus, as compared to syntrophic aceta­
te oxidation and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis, acetoclastic meth­
anogenesis becomes the thermodynamically predominant methane 
pathway and leads to the accumulation of acetic acid, hydrogen, and 
formate molecules in the reactors. Consequently, SPO becomes less 
thermodynamically favorable and jeopardizes the growth of sensitive 
and slow-growing syntrophic propionate oxidizers (Capson-Tojo et al., 
2017) that leads to the formation and accumulation of propionic acid.

cluster and butyric with a thermo-aerobic cluster was attributed to the

High concentrations of short-chain VFAs were measured during the

reduced levels of propionate and increased production of acetate after 
pretreatment accelerated the subsequent methanogenesis as reported by

because its spectrum in both the aerobic and anaerobic pretreatments 
was dominated by butyric and propionic acids which are not a direct 
substrate for the methanogens. On the other hand, a direct correlation

3.3. Effect of pretreatment on microbial diversity and abundance 
In 85 ◦C anaerobic reactors, Firmicutes and Proteobacteria were the 
most dominant phyla accounting for over 98% of total bacterial com­
munity (Fig. 5a). A limited amount of Yersinia and Lactobacillus were 
observed at the genus level in all HRTs except for high amounts of 
Clostridium at an HRT of 3 days (Fig. 5c). However, at such a high 
temperature, it is unlikely that thermophilic microbes would exist 
except for their DNA (Damtie et al., 2020). Therefore, no bacterial ac­
tivity and biodegradation would take place and the pretreatment actions 
from these conditions enhance bioavailability from their thermal effects 
and result in the release of undigested organic macromolecules (carbo­
hydrates and proteins). 
In anaerobic 55 ◦C conditions, hydrolytic fermentative phyla such as 
Thermotogae, Bacteroidetes, Chloroflexi, Cyanobacteria, and Actinobacteria 
were observed to be dominant at all HRTs. Firmicutes play mainly a 
major role in the entire biodegradation activities; Chloroflexi and 
Thermotogae have the metabolic ability to digest carbohydrates while 
Proteobacteria and Bacteriodetes decompose proteins and amino acids 
in syntrophic association with hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Gonza­
lez-Fernandez et al., 2015). High VFAs formation in anaerobic 55 ◦C 
conditions was also linked to Thermotogae and Bacteroidetes. Moreover, 
at the genus level, Clostridium, Sporanaerobacter, Thermogemmatispora, 
Enterococcus, Calothrix, Blautia, and Ruminococcus were detected. Among 
these, Clostridium was found in the highest concentration (over 46%) in 
all HRTs and may be most responsible for the superior biological activity 
and the high tendency of hydrolysis in anaerobic pretreatment at 55 ◦C. 
Clostridia are chemoorganotrophic and saccharolytic fermentative mi­
crobes mainly responsible for the hydrolysis of macromolecules, syn­
trophic acetate oxidation, and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis. This 
is principally because they have cellulosomes, which are extracellular 
complex enzyme systems containing various enzymes such as endoglu­
canases, exoglucanases, hemicellulases, chitinases, pectin lyases, and 
lichenases that can easily degrade lignocellulosic materials to soluble 
monomers (Salakkam et al., 2019). Clostridia are also involved in 
butyrate, acetic acid, lactic acid, and ethanol production due to their 
ability to carry out mixed acid and alcohol fermentation (Magdalena 
et al., 2019). They also contain species such as C. thermocellum that are 
highly thermophilic and cellulolytic and whose spores can survive under 
extreme conditions (Lin et al., 2017). Therefore, these microbes can be 
responsible for the superior biodegradation of carbohydrate macro­
molecules that resulted in either directly forming short-chain VFAs 
(Fig. 2) or indirectly supporting methane yield (Fig. 3a). The high 
biodegradation rate by Clostridia can also be explained using the sCOD 
values. Moreover, high ammonia release in the anaerobic pretreatment 
at 55 ◦C may also be attributable to the proteolytic action of Clostridia 
which accelerated the hydrolysis of proteins into amino acids. E-sup­
plementary data of sCOD values and ammonia release can be found in 
the online version of the paper. These amino acids are then further 
fermented to obtain energy via the Stickland reaction that involves 
coupled oxidation and reduction of amino acids to form VFAs and 
ammonia (Magdalena et al., 2018). Thermogemmatispora and Spor­
anaerobacter were the next most dominant at the genus level. Thermo­
gemmatispora is a cellulolytic and sporulating thermophile having 
excellent nitrate reduction and polysaccharides degradation at high- 
temperatures (Yabe et al., 2017). Sporanaerobacter is a thermophile 
anaerobe that utilizes some sugars, peptides, and various single amino 
acids to form acetic acid (Klassen et al., 2017). Results showed that the 
species observed at HRTs of 1, 2, and 3 days both at the phylum and 
genus level were quite similar (Fig. 5b). This emphasizes the effect of 
HRT in different pretreatment methods. 
In aerobic 55 ◦C conditions, Firmicutes and Proteobacteria were the 
only species responsible for the prevailing biological activities. At the 
genus level, Luteimonas, Symbiobacterium, Soehngenia, Thermobacillus, 
Chromobacterium, and Ureibacillus were dominant. Unlike anaerobic 
pretreatment, significant changes in the microbial community were 
observed with varying HRTs (Fig. 5c green dots) which highlight a 
strong correlation between HRT and microbial diversity in aerobic 
pretreatment. 
At an HRT of 2 days, Ureibacillus and Soehngenia were dominant. 
Ureibacillus (34%) are thermophilic aerobic endospore-forming bacte­
ria capable of high removal of COD and solids by releasing lytic en­
zymes. Their actions include nitrate reduction, starch hydrolysis, and 
acidogenesis from polysaccharides (Fortina et al., 2001). They also 
provide excellent routes for enhancing soluble organic matters (sCOD) 
at shorter HRTs for bioavailability and rapid degradation of organic 
substrates at 55 ◦C at longer HRTs (Liu et al., 2010). The thermos­
phaericus species, Ureibacillus, interestingly, also doesn’t consume 
sugars but decomposes lignocelluloses molecules (Okuda et al., 2008). 
On the other hand, Soehngenia (23%), a carbohydrate degrader, is a 
mesophilic aerotolerant anaerobic bacteria, having saccharolytic and 
weakly proteolytic behavior which also fix molecular nitrogen. Major 
byproducts of fermentation include formate, H2, CO2, acetate, and 
ethanol (Parshina et al., 2003). A marked increase in methane yield 
obtained at an HRT of 2 days (Fig. 3b) perhaps resulted from the initi­
ation of these microbes’ hydrolysis of macromolecules. 
At an HRT of 3 days, Luteimonas, Symbiobacterium, Thermobacillus, 
Ureibacillus were dominant. Luteimonas (23%) are aerobic microbes able 
to reduce nitrate to nitrite while having a negative effect on glucose 
fermentation (Sun et al., 2012). They degrade organic matter degrada­
tion from lignocellulose-rich digestates only at mesophilic conditions 
(Akyol et al., 2019). This genus may make only limited contributions as 
it may not exist at 55 ◦C and has less tendency to facilitate fermentation. 
However, Symbiobacterium (22%) was probably responsible for syntro­
phic relationships with supporting bacteria such as thermophilic Bacillus 
sp. which oxidizes acetate or ethanol to produce energy (Dessì et al., 
2019). Therefore, its significant relative abundance in the aerobic 
reactor can be linked to the prevalence of Ureibacillus (12%) and Ther­
mobacillus (18%) microbes that have substantial ability to degrade. 
Symbiobacterium has been reported to consume various forms of organic 
matter, such as carbohydrates and amino acids and produce L-tyrosine, 
phenol-lyase, and thermostable enzymes responsible for the removal of 
large amounts of sCOD and tCOD as well as facilitating degradation of 
VFAs owing to its tendency to disinhibit acetate degradation (Jin et al., 
2016). The highest VS reduction observed at an HRT of 3 days might be 
attributable to these genera: Symbiobacterium, Thermobacillus and Ure­
ibacillus. Moreover, a substantial amount of Thermobacillus and Clos­
tridium has also been detected in both HRTs. Thermobacillus are aerobic 
thermophiles (up to 72 ◦C) possessing the greatest potential to break­
down lignocellulose and are known as plant biomass degraders. These 
could biodegrade cellulose and polysaccharides to derive energy for 
microbial activities using complex cellulolytic and hemicellulolytic en­
zymes (Lemos et al., 2017). Detection of Clostridium (up to 5% concen­
tration) and some other anaerobes indicates the thermophilic aerobic

4. Conclusions 
sN, sP, sCOD, and propionic acid concentration can serve as reliable 
proxies to optimize and predict the BMP of microalgae biodegradation. 
Total VFAs formation was highly correlated with acetic, butyric acids, 
and removal of VS. Hydrolysis and biomethanization were not corre­
lated during microalgae biodegradation in TPAD. Anaerobic pre­
treatments at 85 ◦C showed excellent performance in releasing 
carbohydrates and proteins, but anaerobic pretreatments at 55 ◦C 
demonstrated high total VFAs due to dominancy of Clostridium. The 
predominance of Luteimonas, Symbiobacterium, Soehngenia, Thermoba­
cillus, and Ureibacillus genera was responsible for VS removal and for­
mation of long-chain VFAs in aerobic pretreatments at 55 ◦C.
